{{Short description|Natural basic set in product spaces}}
{{Lead too short|date=August 2026}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''cylinder sets''' form a [[basis (topology)|basis]] of the [[product topology]] on a product of sets; they are also a generating family of the [[cylinder σ-algebra]].

==General definition==

Given a collection <math>S</math> of sets, consider the [[Cartesian product]] <math display="inline"> X = \prod_{Y\in S} Y</math> of all sets in the collection. The '''canonical projection''' corresponding to some <math>Y\in S</math> is the [[Function (mathematics)|function]] <math>p_{Y} : X \to Y</math> that maps every element of the product to its <math>Y</math> component. A cylinder set is a [[preimage]] of a canonical projection or finite [[Intersection (set theory)|intersection]] of such preimages. Explicitly, it is a set of the form,
<math display="block">\bigcap_{i=1}^n p_{Y_i}^{-1} \left(A_i\right) = \left\{ \left(x\right) \in X \mid p_{Y_1}(x) \in A_1, \dots, p_{Y_n}(x) \in A_n\right\} </math>
for any choice of <math>n</math>, finite sequence of sets <math>Y_1,...Y_n\in S</math> and [[subset]]s <math>A_{i} \subseteq Y_i</math> for <math>1 \leq i \leq n</math>.

Then, when all sets in <math>S</math> are [[topological space]]s, the product topology is [[basis (topology)|generated]] by cylinder sets corresponding to the components' open sets. That is cylinders of the form <math display="inline"> \bigcap_{i=1}^n p_{Y_i}^{-1} \left(U_i\right)</math> where for each <math>i</math>, <math>U_i</math> is open in <math>Y_i</math>. In the same manner, in case of measurable spaces, the [[cylinder σ-algebra]] is the one which is [[Sigma-algebra#σ-algebra generated by an arbitrary family|generated]] by cylinder sets corresponding to the components' measurable sets.

The restriction that the cylinder set be the intersection of a ''finite'' number of open cylinders is important; allowing infinite intersections generally results in a [[Comparison of topologies|finer]] topology. In the latter case, the resulting topology is the [[box topology]]; cylinder sets are never [[Hilbert cube]]s.

==Cylinder sets in products of discrete sets==
Let <math>S = \{1,2,\ldots,n\}</math> be a finite set, containing ''n'' objects or '''letters'''. The collection of all [[bi-infinite string]]s in these letters is denoted by
<math display="block">S^\mathbb{Z} = \{ x = (\ldots, x_{-1}, x_0, x_1, \ldots) : 
x_k \in S \; \forall k \in \mathbb{Z}\}.</math>

The natural topology on <math>S</math> is the [[discrete topology]]. Basic open sets in the discrete topology consist of individual letters; thus, the open cylinders of the product topology on <math>S^\mathbb{Z}</math> are
<math display="block">C_t[a]= \{x \in S^\mathbb{Z} : x_t = a \}.</math>

The intersections of a finite number of open cylinders are the '''cylinder sets'''
<math display="block">\begin{align} 
C_t[a_0, \ldots, a_m] & = C_t[a_0] \,\cap\, C_{t+1}[a_1] \,\cap \cdots \cap\, C_{t+m}[a_m] \\
& = \{x \in S^\mathbb{Z} : x_t = a_0, \ldots ,x_{t+m} = a_m \}
\end{align}.</math>

Cylinder sets are [[clopen set]]s. As elements of the topology, cylinder sets are by definition open sets. The complement of an open set is a closed set, but the complement of a cylinder set is a [[Union (set theory)|union]] of cylinders, and so cylinder sets are also closed, and are thus clopen.

==Definition for vector spaces==

Given a finite or infinite-[[Dimension (vector space)|dimensional]] [[vector space]] <math>V</math> over a [[Field (mathematics)|field]] ''K'' (such as the [[Real number|real]] or [[complex number]]s), the cylinder sets may be defined as
<math display="block">C_A[f_1, \ldots, f_n] = \{x \in V : (f_1(x),f_2(x),\ldots,f_n(x)) \in A \}</math>
where <math>A \subset K^n</math> is a [[Borel set]] in <math>K^n</math>, and each <math>f_j</math> is a [[linear functional]] on <math>V</math>; that is, <math>f_j\in (V^*)^{\otimes n}</math>, the [[Dual space#Algebraic dual space|algebraic dual space]] to <math>V</math>. When dealing with [[topological vector space]]s, the definition is made instead for elements <math>f_j \in (V')^{\otimes n}</math>, the [[Dual space#Continuous dual space|continuous dual space]]. That is, the functionals <math>f_j</math> are taken to be continuous linear functionals.

==Applications==
Cylinder sets are often used to define a topology on sets that are subsets of <math>S^\mathbb{Z}</math> and occur frequently in the study of [[symbolic dynamics]]; see, for example, [[subshift of finite type]]. Cylinder sets are often used to define a [[measure theory|measure]], using the [[Kolmogorov extension theorem]]; for example, the measure of a cylinder set of length ''m'' might be given by {{math|1/''m''}} or by {{math|1/2<sup>''m''</sup>}}. 

Cylinder sets may be used to define a [[Metric (mathematics)|metric]] on the space: for example, one says that two strings are '''ε-close''' if a fraction 1−ε of the letters in the strings match.

Since strings in <math>S^\mathbb{Z}</math> can be considered to be [[p-adic number|''p''-adic numbers]], some of the theory of ''p''-adic numbers can be applied to cylinder sets, and in particular, the definition of [[p-adic measure|''p''-adic measures]] and [[p-adic metric|''p''-adic metrics]] apply to cylinder sets. These types of measure spaces appear in the theory of [[dynamical systems]] and are called [[nonsingular odometer]]s. A generalization of these systems is the [[Markov odometer]]. 

Cylinder sets over topological vector spaces are the core ingredient in the{{Citation needed|date=January 2022}} definition of [[abstract Wiener space]]s, which provide the formal definition of the [[Feynman path integral]] or [[functional integral]] of [[quantum field theory]], and the [[Partition function (mathematics)|partition function]] of [[statistical mechanics]].
